title: DeferKV: Rethinking Eviction Timing for One-Shot KV Cache Compression

paper.title: DeferKV: Rethinking Eviction Timing for One-Shot KV Cache Compression
paper.abstract:
Abstract Long-context large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, but the growing KV cache
introduces substantial memory and inference overhead. Existing one-shot KV cache compression methods typically commit to irreversible eviction immediately after prefill, before any signal from actual generation becomes available. Our quantitative analysis shows that early queries from the actual generation stage provide attention signals that are more consistent with subsequent decode attention, with the largest single-step gain occurring at the prefill–decode boundary. Based on this observation, we propose DeferKV, which moves the eviction decision from the end of prefill to the first real decoding step and temporally combines prompt-side and decode-side observations, thereby better aligning KV importance estimation with subsequent generation requirements. DeferKV requires no additional
training, draft model, or future-query prediction module, making it simple and easy to deploy.
Experiments on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack demonstrate
that DeferKV consistently improves model performance under KV cache
compression while maintaining low inference latency.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large language models (LLMs) with long-context capabilities OpenAI (2023) ; Team (2025) have demonstrated strong performance in document question answering Dasigi et al. (2021) , multi-document summarization Fabbri et al. (2019) , code understanding Bai et al. (2024) , retrieval-augmented generation Lewis et al. (2020) , and complex reasoning Yao et al. (2023) . However, long-context inference also introduces substantial system overhead. In particular, the KV cache has become a major bottleneck affecting memory consumption and inference throughput Li et al. (2025) ; Shi et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2024) . For autoregressive Transformer decoders Vaswani et al. (2017) , the key and value representations of historical tokens must be cached at every layer to avoid redundant computation during generation. As the context length increases, the memory consumption of the KV cache grows linearly with the sequence length, making long-context inference more challenging on memory-constrained devices and in high-concurrency serving scenarios. Therefore, compressing the KV cache while preserving generation quality has become an important research problem in efficient LLM inference. Existing KV cache compression methods often perform one-time KV eviction immediately after the prefill stage. Representative methods such as SnapKV Li et al. (2024) use a small set of queries near the end of the prompt as an observation window and estimate the importance of historical tokens based on the attention scores between these queries and historical keys, thereby selecting the KV tokens to retain. These methods are simple to implement, require no additional training, and offer favorable efficiency in practice. Figure 1: Consistency of prompt-end and first-decode attention with subsequent decode attention on GovReport using Qwen3-8B. Each point denotes a historical KV token. The horizontal axis shows its average attention from D 2 D_{2} to the end of generation, while the vertical axis shows the average over the last 32 prefill queries and the attention from the first decode query. The dashed diagonal marks exact agreement, and the shaded region indicates values within a factor of two. However, these methods Li et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025) typically rely on a key assumption: the queries within the observation window at the end of the prompt are sufficient to reflect the actual attention requirements of subsequent decoding. This assumption does not always hold in long-text generation tasks. As shown in Figure 1 , more historical KV tokens lie closer to the diagonal when using the first real decode query. Its attention scores are therefore more consistent with subsequent decode attention than those aggregated from the final 32 prefill queries. This suggests that prompt-end attention alone may not fully capture the access patterns observed during subsequent generation. Consequently, estimating KV importance solely from prompt-side queries may lead to suboptimal token selection for later decoding. Recent methods have begun to address this issue by incorporating information related to future generation into KV token importance estimation. For example, SpecKV Galim et al. (2026) , LAQ Wang et al. (2025) , and LookaheadKV Ahn et al. (2026) construct or predict future queries or attention patterns to make KV compression more closely aligned with the requirements of the actual generation stage. Although these methods alleviate the limitations of prompt-only observation from different perspectives, they usually require additional models, auxiliary modules, or extra training procedures and inevitably face uncertainty introduced by prediction errors. Based on these observations, we propose a more direct and lightweight approach. Unlike existing methods that rely solely on prompt-side information, our strategy postpones irreversible KV eviction until the first real decode-side signal becomes available and incorporates a small amount of attention feedback from actual generation. This explicitly aligns the importance estimation of historical tokens with the requirements of subsequent decoding. We further consider how to effectively integrate observations from the input and generation stages. To this end, we introduce a simple yet effective temporal weighting strategy to improve the reliability and accuracy of importance estimation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We revisit the timing assumption of existing KV cache compression methods that perform eviction immediately after prefill. We propose a compression approach that postpones irreversible KV eviction until the earliest real decode-side feedback becomes available, thereby better aligning KV selection with subsequent decoding. • Our method is simple, direct, and lightweight. It does not require additional training, a draft model, an auxiliary network, or a future-query prediction module. It only requires minor modifications to the existing inference process, enabling straightforward implementation and deployment. • Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving relative performance gains of up to 3.58% on LongBench and 8.03% on RULER.

sections.heading: 2.1 KV Cache Compression and Token Eviction
sections.text: To reduce the memory consumption of the KV cache, existing studies Zhang et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023) have explored compression by reducing the number of cached tokens. These methods typically retain important Key-Value pairs according to the potential contribution of historical tokens to subsequent generation, while evicting KV entries with lower importance, thereby controlling the cache size during decoding. Prompt-only compression methods usually perform a one-time selection of prompt KV tokens after the prefill stage and before decoding begins Li et al. (2025) . They are generally simple to implement and introduce limited scheduling overhead. SnapKV Li et al. (2024) uses an observation window near the end of the prompt to estimate the importance of historical KV tokens and selects clustered important KV positions within each attention head. PyramidKV Cai et al. (2024) further considers layer-wise budget allocation and assigns larger cache budgets to lower layers and smaller budgets to higher layers according to their different information aggregation characteristics. Ada-KV Feng et al. (2025) focuses on the importance differences across attention heads and adaptively allocates more cache capacity to heads that have a greater influence on the model output. ChunkKV Liu et al. (2025) treats semantic chunks rather than individual tokens as the basic compression units and introduces layer-wise index reuse to preserve contextual integrity while reducing selection overhead. These methods rely primarily on prompt-side observations and may not fully reflect the actual attention requirements of subsequent decoding.

sections.heading: 2.2 Future-Aware KV Cache Compression
sections.text: To alleviate the limitations of prompt-only observation, recent studies have begun to introduce future-aware signals. These methods improve KV selection by predicting or approximating future queries, making the compression strategy more closely aligned with the requirements of the actual generation stage. SpecKV Galim et al. (2026) uses a lightweight draft model to generate approximate future tokens and employs these lookahead tokens to help the target model estimate the importance of prompt KV pairs for subsequent generation. LAQ Wang et al. (2025) performs low-budget lookahead decoding after prefill to generate a small number of pseudo-response tokens. It then caches their corresponding query states as a Q-Cache and uses them to re-evict the KV cache. LookaheadKV Ahn et al. (2026) further introduces learnable lookahead tokens and combines them with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) modules to predict future attention patterns, thereby obtaining future-aware signals for KV selection. Although these methods better align KV compression with generation requirements, they generally introduce additional model components, training procedures, or inference overhead, increasing system complexity and deployment cost.

sections.heading: 3.2 Obs. 1: Prefill-to-Decode Attention Shift
sections.text: As shown in Figure 2 , prefill queries already show moderate consistency with the reference attention distribution, indicating that prompt-side attention contains useful signals for KV importance estimation Li et al. (2024) . However, moving from the final prefill query at r = − 1 r=-1 to the first real decode query at r = 1 r=1 increases JSD-Based Similarity and KV Selection Recall by 0.056 0.056 and 0.052 0.052 , respectively. This sharp improvement indicates that the first real decode query reveals generation-specific access requirements that are not fully captured during prefill, making it a more reliable signal for KV importance estimation.

sections.heading: 3.3 Obs. 2: Largest Gain at First Decode
sections.text: Among all adjacent query positions, the largest single-step gain occurs at the prefill–decode boundary. In comparison, the average gains between adjacent subsequent decode positions are only 0.009 0.009 for JSD-Based Similarity and 0.007 0.007 for KV Selection Recall, both substantially lower than those at the boundary. Later decode queries can further improve consistency with the reference attention distribution. However, using these later queries requires retaining the full prompt KV cache for additional decode steps, thereby increasing memory usage and end-to-end inference latency. Therefore, the first real decode query provides the earliest decode-side observation with the largest gain, offering a favorable trade-off between KV selection quality and system overhead. Figure 3: Overview of DeferKV. The first real decode query is combined with recent prompt queries and temporally weighted to estimate KV importance for subsequent cache compression.

sections.heading: 3.4 Obs. 3: Temporal Relevance Decay
sections.text: Beyond the improvement at the prefill–decode boundary, both metrics generally increase as query positions approach the decode stage. Although the trend is not strictly monotonic, earlier prefill queries are typically less consistent with the reference attention distribution. This suggests that queries contribute differently to KV importance estimation. We therefore assign larger weights to queries closer to the decode stage and gradually discount earlier queries, emphasizing generation-related signals while preserving prompt-side context.

sections.heading: 4.1 Overall Workflow
sections.text: Prompt-side attention does not fully reflect the KV access requirements of subsequent decoding, while the first real decode query provides a more reliable signal and queries closer to decoding are generally more informative. Based on these observations, DeferKV postpones KV cache compression until after the first standard decoding step. As illustrated in Figure 3 , DeferKV obtains the first real decode query from the target model and combines it with recent prompt queries to form a decode-aware observation window. Their attention scores are aggregated using temporal weighting, assigning greater importance to queries closer to the decode stage. The resulting scores are used to estimate prompt-token importance and construct the compressed KV cache for subsequent generation. In this way, DeferKV better aligns KV selection with actual decoding requirements without predicting future queries, introducing auxiliary models, or altering the standard generation trajectory.

Our method only changes the timing of the initial KV cache compression and reuses the query naturally produced during the target model’s decoding process. Therefore, it requires no modification to the model architecture or additional training procedure.

sections.heading: Selected Baselines.
sections.text: We compare against four representative KV cache compression methods: (1) SnapKV Li et al. (2024) , which estimates historical KV importance using a local observation window near the end of the prompt and performs one-time compression before decoding; (2) LAQ Wang et al. (2025) , which performs low-budget lookahead decoding with an initially compressed cache and uses the resulting query states to guide a second KV eviction; (3) SpecKV Galim et al. (2026) , which uses a small draft model to generate a proxy response and processes it with the target model to estimate prompt-KV importance; (4) LookaheadKV Ahn et al. (2026) , which uses learnable lookahead tokens and lightweight LoRA modules to estimate prompt-KV importance.

sections.heading: Implementation Details.
sections.text: We evaluate DeferKV and all baselines under varying cache budgets ( B total = n ​ L B_{\mathrm{total}}=nL , with n ∈ [ 64 , 1024 ] n\in[64,1024] ), where n n is the prompt KV budget for each layer and L L is the number of layers. We use greedy decoding without sampling for all experiments to ensure deterministic and reproducible evaluation. We use the official baseline implementations with standard eviction settings, with further details provided in Appendix B . All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 80 GB of memory.

sections.heading: 5.2 Results on LongBench
sections.text: We evaluate DeferKV on 16 LongBench datasets using three language models. Table 1 reports detailed results under a tight cache budget of B total = 64 ​ L B_{\mathrm{total}}=64L and a larger cache budget of B total = 512 ​ L B_{\mathrm{total}}=512L . DeferKV achieves the highest average score across all six model–budget settings. Under the tight 64 ​ L 64L budget, DeferKV consistently ranks as the top-performing method across models, achieving up to a 3.58% relative improvement over the strongest baseline with Qwen3-8B. This advantage is particularly pronounced under constrained cache budgets, where real decode feedback improves KV importance estimation and helps preserve information essential for subsequent generation. As the budget increases to B total = 512 ​ L B_{\mathrm{total}}=512L , the performance gaps among methods narrow because more prompt KV tokens can be retained. Nevertheless, DeferKV continues to achieve the best average performance and approaches Full KV across all three models. In addition to its strong performance, DeferKV requires no additional training, draft model, or future-query prediction module, making it simple to implement and deploy. We further integrate DeferKV with PyramidKV, AdaKV, and ChunkKV to demonstrate its compatibility with existing KV cache compression methods. The corresponding results are provided in Appendix D .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we revisit a basic design choice in one-shot KV cache compression: when to commit to irreversible eviction. DeferKV moves this decision to the first decoding step, where real generation-side feedback becomes available, and uses temporal weighting to integrate the first real decode query with recent prompt queries. Extensive evaluations on LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and RULER show that DeferKV improves long-context performance with low inference latency. It requires no additional training, draft model, or auxiliary prediction module, providing a lightweight approach to efficient long-context inference.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: DeferKV postpones one-shot KV eviction until the earliest real decode query becomes available, which requires retaining the full prompt KV cache through the first decoding step. This design therefore shifts the memory reduction to subsequent decoding. Our experiments focus on models with standard token-wise KV caches under softmax attention. Extending DeferKV to architectures with different cache organizations, such as MLA or hybrid linear-attention models, may require architecture-specific adaptation.

sections.heading: DeferKV.
sections.text: We use an observation-window size of W = 32 W=32 , a temporal discount factor of η = 0.7 \eta=0.7 , and average pooling with kernel size 5 5 . Compression is performed after the first standard decode step ( d = 1 d=1 ). The aggregate prompt-KV budget is B total = n ​ L B_{\mathrm{total}}=nL , where n n is the retained prompt-KV budget per layer and L L is the number of model layers.

sections.heading: SnapKV.
sections.text: The final 32 prompt queries are used as the observation window. Importance scores are smoothed by average pooling with kernel size 5 5 , after which the highest-ranked prompt KV pairs are retained under the target budget.

sections.heading: LAQ.
sections.text: Starting from a temporary KV cache obtained by applying SnapKV to the original prompt cache, the target model performs up to eight lookahead decoding steps and stores the corresponding query states in the Q-Cache. These lookahead queries, together with the final eight prompt queries, are then used to recompute the attention-based importance scores of the original prompt KV entries before the second eviction.

sections.heading: SpecKV.
sections.text: The draft models are Qwen3-0.6B for Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct for Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and mistral-7b-instruct-v0.3-bnb-4bit for Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3. The target-model queries corresponding to the prompt observation window and the generated draft tokens are used to rank historical prompt KV pairs. In the reproduction, the resulting importance scores are smoothed using average pooling with kernel size 5 5 .

sections.heading: LookaheadKV.
sections.text: LookaheadKV is configured with 32 learnable lookahead tokens, and a separate set of lookahead modules is trained for each target model. The training data consist of 50K samples from ChatQA2-Long-SFT-data and 20K from tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture. The predicted importance scores are smoothed using average pooling with kernel size 5 5 before prompt-KV selection.

sections.heading: Common Settings.
sections.text: All methods use random seed 42. Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 are evaluated using their official checkpoints, tokenizers, and prompt templates. Greedy decoding with batch size one is used. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 80 GB GPUs.

sections.heading: Appendix G Numerical Analysis of Compression Delay Steps
sections.text: The results reported in the main paper show that increasing the compression delay provides only modest performance improvements. Compared with d = 1 d=1 , using d = 2 d=2 increases the task score from 27.06 to 27.11, corresponding to a relative improvement of only 0.18 % 0.18\% , while end-to-end latency increases from 11.562 to 11.618 seconds, or 0.48 % 0.48\% . Therefore, waiting for a second decode query introduces an additional full-cache decoding step but produces only a negligible improvement in the final task score. The same trade-off remains as the delay is increased further. At d = 4 d=4 , the score improves by only 0.55 % 0.55\% relative to d = 1 d=1 , whereas latency increases by 1.63 % 1.63\% . Peak memory remains nearly unchanged across the evaluated settings. These results suggest that additional decode observations can slightly refine KV importance estimation, but the improvement is not large enough to justify postponing compression. We therefore use d = 1 d=1 , which incorporates real decode feedback at the earliest available step while avoiding unnecessary full-cache decoding overhead.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.06286v1 [cs.CL] 05 Oct 2026 DeferKV: Rethinking Eviction Timing for One-Shot KV Cache Compression Zhe Wang Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China Affiliation: Ubiquitous Intelligence and Trusted Services Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China Jiakai Li Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China Affiliation: Ubiquitous Intelligence and Trusted Services Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China Yujia Sun Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China Affiliation: Ubiquitous Intelligence and Trusted Services Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China Rongzheng Wang Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China Affiliation: Ubiquitous Intelligence and Trusted Services Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China Shuang Liang † † thanks: Corresponding author: shuangliang@uestc.edu.cn Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China Affiliation: Ubiquitous Intelligence and Trusted Services Key Laboratory of Sichuan Province, Chengdu, China Abstract Long-context large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities across a wide range of tasks, but the growing KV cache introduces substantial memory and inference overhead. Existing one-shot KV cache compression methods typically commit to irreversible eviction immediately after prefill, before any signal from actual generation becomes available. Our quantitative analysis shows that early queries from the actual generation stage provide attention signals that are more consistent with subsequent decode attention, with the largest single-step gain occurring at the prefill–decode boundary. Based on this observation, we propose DeferKV, which moves the eviction decision from the end of prefill to the first real decoding step and temporally combines prompt-side and decode-side observations, thereby better aligning KV importance estimation with subsequent generation requirements. DeferKV requires no additional training, draft model, or future-query prediction module, making it simple and easy to deploy. Experiments on LongBench, RULER, and Needle-in-a-Haystack demonstrate that DeferKV consistently improves model performance under KV cache compression while maintaining low inference latency. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) with long-context capabilities OpenAI (2023) ; Team (2025) have demonstrated strong performance in document question answering Dasigi et al. (2021) , multi-document summarization Fabbri et al. (2019) , code understanding Bai et al. (2024) , retrieval-augmented generation Lewis et al. (2020) , and complex reasoning Yao et al. (2023) . However, long-context inference also introduces substantial system overhead. In particular, the KV cache has become a major bottleneck affecting memory consumption and inference throughput Li et al. (2025) ; Shi et al. (2024) ; Yuan et al. (2024) . For autoregressive Transformer decoders Vaswani et al. (2017) , the key and value representations of historical tokens must be cached at every layer to avoid redundant computation during generation. As the context length increases, the memory consumption of the KV cache grows linearly with the sequence length, making long-context inference more challenging on memory-constrained devices and in high-concurrency serving scenarios. Therefore, compressing the KV cache while preserving generation quality has become an important research problem in efficient LLM inference. Existing KV cache compression methods often perform one-time KV eviction immediately after the prefill stage. Representative methods such as SnapKV Li et al. (2024) use a small set of queries near the end of the prompt as an observation window and estimate the importance of historical tokens based on the attention scores between these queries and historical keys, thereby selecting the KV tokens to retain. These methods are simple to implement, require no additional training, and offer favorable efficiency in practice. Figure 1: Consistency of prompt-end and first-decode attention with subsequent decode attention on GovReport using Qwen3-8B. Each point denotes a historical KV token. The horizontal axis shows its average attention from D 2 D_{2} to the end of generation, while the vertical axis shows the average over the last 32 prefill queries and the attention from the first decode query. The dashed diagonal marks exact agreement, and the shaded region indicates values within a factor of two. However, these methods Li et al. (2024) ; Liu et al. (2025) typically rely on a key assumption: the queries within the observation window at the end of the prompt are sufficient to reflect the actual attention requirements of subsequent decoding. This assumption does not always hold in long-text generation tasks. As shown in Figure 1 , more historical KV tokens lie closer to the diagonal when using the first real decode query. Its attention scores are therefore more consistent with subsequent decode attention than those aggregated from the final 32 prefill queries. This suggests that prompt-end attention alone may not fully capture the access patterns observed during subsequent generation. Consequently, estimating KV importance solely from prompt-side queries may lead to suboptimal token selection for later decoding. Recent methods have begun to address this issue by incorporating information related to future generation into KV token importance estimation. For example, SpecKV Galim et al. (2026) , LAQ Wang et al. (2025) , and LookaheadKV Ahn et al. (2026) construct or predict future queries or attention patterns to make KV compression more closely aligned with the requirements of the actual generation stage. Although these methods alleviate the limitations of prompt-only observation from different perspectives, they usually require additional models, auxiliary modules, or extra training procedures and inevitably face uncertainty introduced by prediction errors. Based on these observations, we propose a more direct and lightweight approach. Unlike existing methods that rely solely on prompt-side information, our strategy postpones irreversible KV eviction until the first real decode-side signal becomes available and incorporates a small amount of attention feedback from actual generation. This explicitly aligns the importance estimation of historical tokens with the requirements of subsequent decoding. We further consider how to effectively integrate observations from the input and generation stages. To this end, we introduce a simple yet effective temporal weighting strategy to improve the reliability and accuracy of importance estimation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We revisit the timing assumption of existing KV cache compression methods that perform eviction immediately after prefill. We propose a compression approach that postpones irreversible KV eviction until the earliest real decode-side feedback becomes available, thereby better aligning KV selection with subsequent decoding. • Our method is simple, direct, and lightweight. It does not require additional training, a draft model, an auxiliary network, or a future-query prediction module. It only requires minor modifications to the existing inference process, enabling straightforward implementation and deployment. • Extensive experiments show that our method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines under constrained KV cache budgets, achieving relative performance gains of up to 3.58% on LongBench and 8.03% on RULER. 2 Related Work 2.1 KV Cache Compression and Token Eviction To reduce the memory consumption of the KV cache, existing studies Zhang et al. (2023) ; Liu et al. (2023) have explored compression by reducing the number of cached tokens. These methods typically retain important Key-Value pairs according to the potential contribution of historical tokens to subsequent generation, while evicting KV entries with lower importance, thereby controlling the cache size during decoding. Prompt-only compression methods usually perform a one-time selection of prompt KV tokens after the prefill stage and before decoding begins Li et al. (2025) . They are generally simple to implement and introduce limited scheduling overhead. SnapKV Li et al. (2024) uses an observation window near the end of the prompt to estimate the importance of historical KV tokens and selects clustered important KV positions within each attention head. PyramidKV Cai et al. (2024) further considers layer-wise budget allocation and assigns larger cache budgets to lower layers and smaller budgets to higher layers according to their different information aggregation characteristics. Ada-KV Feng et al. (2025) focuses on the importance differences across attention heads and adaptively allocates more cache capacity to heads that have a greater influence on the model output. ChunkKV Liu et al. (2025) treats semantic chunks rather than individual tokens as the basic compression units and introduces layer-wise index reuse to preserve contextual integrity while reducing selection overhead. These methods rely primarily on prompt-side observations and may not fully reflect the actual attention requirements of subsequent decoding. 2.2 Future-Aware KV Cache Compression To alleviate the limitations of prompt-only observation, recent studies have begun to introduce future-aware signals. These methods improve KV selection by predicting or approximating future queries, making the compression strategy more closely aligned with the requirements of the actual generation stage. SpecKV Galim et al. (2026) uses a lightweight draft model to generate approximate future tokens and employs these lookahead tokens to help the target model estimate the importance of prompt KV pairs for subsequent generation. LAQ Wang et al. (2025) performs low-budget lookahead decoding after prefill to generate a small number of pseudo-response tokens. It then caches their corresponding query states as a Q-Cache and uses them to re-evict the KV cache. LookaheadKV Ahn et al. (2026) further introduces learnable lookahead tokens and combines them with LoRA Hu et al. (2022) modules to predict future attention patterns, thereby obtaining future-aware signals for KV selection. Although these methods better align KV compression with generation requirements, they generally introduce additional model components, training procedures, or inference overhead, increasing system complexity and deployment cost. 3 Observations To characterize the transition from prompt-side observations to actual decode-stage access patterns, we compare the attention distributions produced by queries at different positions with a reference attention distribution constructed from later decode queries. We consider both distributional similarity and the overlap between their induced KV-token selections. Specifically, we evaluate the final 32 32 prefill queries and the first 8 8 real decode queries, with relative positions r ∈ { − 32 , − 31 , … , − 1 , 1 , 2 , … , 8 } . r\in\{-32,-31,\ldots,-1,1,2,\ldots,8\}. (2021) , MultiNews Fabbri et al. (2019) , QMSum Zhong et al. (2021) , and RepoBench-P Liu et al. (2024b) . For each model–task combination, we randomly sample 30 30 examples, resulting in 360 360 evaluation instances in total. The KV budget is set to B = 512 B=512 . For each sample, we perform the complete generation process under the FullKV setting. Based on these observations, DeferKV postpones KV cache compression until after the first standard decoding step. As illustrated in Figure 3 , DeferKV obtains the first real decode query from the target model and combines it with recent prompt queries to form a decode-aware observation window. Their attention scores are aggregated using temporal weighting, assigning greater importance to queries closer to the decode stage. The resulting scores are used to estimate prompt-token importance and construct the compressed KV cache for subsequent generation. DeferKV moves this decision to the first decoding step, where real generation-side feedback becomes available, and uses temporal weighting to integrate the first real decode query with recent prompt queries. Extensive evaluations on LongBench, Needle-in-a-Haystack, and RULER show that DeferKV improves long-context performance with low inference latency. It requires no additional training, draft model, or auxiliary prediction module, providing a lightweight approach to efficient long-context inference. Limitations DeferKV postpones one-shot KV eviction until the earliest real decode query becomes available, which requires retaining the full prompt KV cache through the first decoding step. This design therefore shifts the memory reduction to subsequent decoding. Our experiments focus on models with standard token-wise KV caches under softmax attention. Extending DeferKV to architectures with different cache organizations, such as MLA or hybrid linear-attention models, may require architecture-specific adaptation. References Ahn et al. (2026) J.
